questions.prompt: A user's group policy allows `s3:*` on a bucket. Their own inline policy denies `s3:DeleteObject` on the same bucket. What happens when they delete an object?
choices: Allowed, because group policies take precedence over user policies
Allowed, because `s3:*` is more general and was attached first
Denied, because an explicit Deny in any applicable policy ends evaluation, whatever else allows
It depends on which of the two policies was created more recently
questions.explanation: AWS first looks for a Deny that applies, across every policy type. One match gives explicitDeny. Order of attachment, specificity and where the policy is attached play no part.

questions.prompt: A role in account 111111111111 has `AdministratorAccess`. Writing to a bucket in account 222222222222 fails with `because no resource-based policy allows the s3:PutObject action`. What fixes it with the least access?
choices: Ask for the SCP on account 111111111111 to be removed
Attach `AmazonS3FullAccess` to the role as well
Change the bucket policy's principal to `"*"`
Add a statement to the bucket's policy in 222222222222 that allows that role's ARN `s3:PutObject` on the objects it writes
questions.explanation: A cross-account request is evaluated in both accounts. The caller's side already allows (administrator access), and the resource account's policy is the gate that failed, as the message says. A principal of `*` would open the bucket far wider than one role.

questions.prompt: A role's policies allow `s3:*`, its permissions boundary allows only `s3:List*`, and the session was created with a session policy that allows `s3:GetObject`. Which call succeeds?
choices: `s3:GetObject`, because the session policy names it explicitly
Neither `s3:GetObject` nor `s3:ListBucket`: every action must be allowed by the identity policy, the boundary and the session policy, and no action is allowed by all three
`s3:ListBucket`, because the boundary allows it
Both, because the identity policy allows `s3:*`
questions.explanation: Identity-based policies, the boundary and the session policy intersect. `s3:GetObject` fails the boundary, and `s3:ListBucket` fails the session policy. None of the three grants anything the others do not.

questions.prompt: An Allow statement has `"Condition": {"ForAllValues:StringEquals": {"aws:TagKeys": ["env", "team"]}}` on `ec2:CreateTags`. A caller sends a request that carries no tags at all. What does the condition evaluate to?
choices: True: `ForAllValues` holds when the key is absent, so the statement applies. Add `"Null": {"aws:TagKeys": "false"}` to require tags
An error: the request is rejected as malformed
False, because `ForAllValues` needs at least one value to compare
False, because the key is missing
questions.explanation: The IAM documentation says ForAllValues returns true when the key is missing or empty. That makes Allow statements wider than they read. Access Analyzer flags it, and so does `iameval validate`.

questions.prompt: In one account, a bucket policy allows `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"}` to `s3:GetObject`. The user `analyst` in that account has no identity-based policies. Can they read objects?
choices: No: naming the account delegates to identity-based policies, so the user needs their own Allow. A grant that named the user's ARN would stand on its own
Yes, because the account principal includes every user in the account
Yes, but only from the AWS console
No, because bucket policies never apply to principals in the bucket owner's account
questions.explanation: An account principal grants the account, and the account's administrator still has to grant the identity. In the same account, a resource-based policy works on its own only when it names the IAM user or the role session directly (or `*`).

questions.prompt: Your tests run against moto with IAM enforcement on and pass. Which statement about production is correct?
choices: Production will behave the same, because moto implements IAM
Production will be stricter only for SCPs

The tests proved identity-based allows and denies. moto does not enforce permissions boundaries, session policies, conditions outside trust policies or policy variables, and it never lets a bucket policy grant, so check those against AWS's evaluation logic or the policy simulator
Nothing can be concluded, because moto ignores IAM entirely
questions.explanation: moto checks signatures and identity-based policies for the principals it issued keys to, and role trust policies with a limited `StringEquals`. The smoke test records exactly six request types where it differs from AWS, and those need fixtures from the documentation or a real simulator.
